cards.front: What does a p-value actually measure?
cards.back: The **probability**, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of getting a sample result at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the chance the null hypothesis is true.
cards.hint: Start by assuming the null is true.

cards.front: What are the three parts of a correct p-value interpretation, in order?
cards.back: 1) Assume the null hypothesis is true, using the claimed value in context. 2) Describe a sample result at least as extreme as the one observed. 3) Give the **probability** and say it comes from random sampling.
cards.hint: Three steps, always in this order.

cards.front: What does a small p-value tell you about the null hypothesis?
cards.back: It is **strong evidence against** the null hypothesis, because the result would be unusual if the null were true. A large p-value gives weak evidence against it.
cards.hint: Think about how surprising the result would be.

cards.front: Where does the p-value come from on the null model curve?
cards.back: It is the **area in the tail** beyond your observed result. A result far out in the tail leaves little area, giving a small p-value.
cards.hint: Picture the bell curve centered on the null value.

cards.front: How is a two-sided p-value found from a one-tail area?
cards.back: It is **double** the one-tail area, because a two-sided alternative counts both tails of the null model.

cards.front: A shop claims 40% of customers use a loyalty card. 47% of 200 sampled do; one-sided p-value 0.022. Interpret the p-value in context.
cards.back: If exactly 40% of all customers use a loyalty card, there is about a **2.2% chance** that a random sample of 200 customers has 47% or more users.
cards.hint: Assume the claim is true first.

cards.back: A **cutoff** set before seeing the data. A p-value at or below $\alpha$ is statistically significant. Common choices are 0.05 and 0.01.
cards.hint: It is chosen before you look at the data.

cards.front: Is a p-value of 0.03 the chance that the null hypothesis is true?
cards.back: **No.** The p-value assumes the null is true and describes how likely the data are under that assumption. It says nothing about the probability the null is true.
cards.hint: Which hypothesis is assumed true here?

cards.front: Does a large p-value prove the null hypothesis is true?
cards.back: **No.** A large p-value means the result is not unusual, so the evidence against the null is weak. Never say the null is proven true or false.
cards.hint: Weak evidence is not the same as proof.

cards.back: Whether the size of a difference or effect is **large enough to matter** in the real situation. The p-value alone cannot answer this.
cards.hint: Think about real life, not statistics.

cards.front: Why can a huge sample give a small p-value for a tiny difference?
cards.back: Sample size drives the gap: a very large sample can make even a tiny difference statistically significant, while a tiny difference may still not matter in real life.
cards.hint: Consider 40,000 users with a 50.5% success rate.

cards.front: A p-value is 0.001. Does this show the effect is large?
cards.back: **No.** A small p-value shows only that the result is unlikely to be random variation alone, not that the effect is large.
cards.hint: Separate significance from size of the effect.
